name: Samantabhadra
role: Bodhisattva of vows, practice and good deeds
summary: Samantabhadra is a Mahayana bodhisattva whose name means "All Good". He is linked to the ten great vows and is usually shown on a white elephant with six tusks.
about: In Mahayana Buddhism, Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice and compassionate action. The Avatamsaka Sutra tells that he spoke ten great vows that became a model for the bodhisattva path, and the Lotus Sutra tradition honours him as its patron. He often stands beside Shakyamuni, with Manjushri on the other side, as a trio called the Shakyamuni Triad. East Asian art shows him riding a six-tusked white elephant. Tibetan Nyingma teachers also use the same name for a different figure, the primordial Buddha Kuntuzangpo. This profile follows the bodhisattva, and the story below comes from the Gandavyuha section of the Avatamsaka Sutra.
kidSummary: Samantabhadra is a kind helper in Buddhist stories who teaches that good wishes must become good actions. He rides a gentle white elephant with six tusks. People remember him when they want to help others, say sorry, and share the good they have done.

story.title: A boy begins a journey
story.text: In the Gandavyuha, a young seeker named Sudhana is sent by Manjushri to find teachers who can show him the way to wisdom.

story.title: Fifty-odd teachers
story.text: Sudhana travels from place to place and learns something new from each teacher he meets, from merchants and healers to kings and children.

story.title: Meeting Maitreya
story.text: Near the end he meets Maitreya, who shows him a great tower that holds endless wonders, and sends him back to Manjushri.

story.title: Samantabhadra appears
story.text: Sudhana finally meets Samantabhadra, who confirms how far he has come. In the text, Sudhana then becomes one with Samantabhadra.

story.title: Ten vows of good conduct
story.text: Samantabhadra gives ten vows: honour the Buddhas, give offerings, say sorry for mistakes, enjoy the good of others, and share all your goodness with every living being.

teaches: Good wishes should turn into action
Rejoice in the goodness of others
Share the good you do with all beings

facts.text: The Huayan school honours Samantabhadra, Manjushri and the Buddha Vairocana together as the Three Noble Ones, with the two bodhisattvas standing on either side of Vairocana.
Borobudur in Java carries carvings of Sudhana's search. The monument has 2,672 relief panels in all, and 1,460 of them tell stories.
Some believers say his white elephant is the same one that appeared to Queen Maya to herald the Buddha's birth.
In the novel Investiture of the Gods, his Daoist form Puxian Zhenren is master of Muzha, Nezha's elder brother, and gives him a pair of Wu Gou swords.
Before Mount Emei became Samantabhadra's seat, it was a Daoist sacred site with temples and hermits, and local tradition links Puxian with both Buddhist and Daoist traits.
In the 16th-century novel Investiture of the Gods, the foe Lingya Xian is beaten and shows his true shape, a six-tusked white elephant, which becomes Puxian's mount.
Chinese art sometimes shows Puxian with feminine features, riding a six-tusked elephant and carrying a lotus-leaf parasol, a ruyi sceptre or a scroll, much like some images of Guanyin.
A Japanese painting type, Fugen and the Ten Demonesses, shows him on a six-tusked elephant with ten guardian demonesses who protect those who follow the Lotus Sutra.
In the Gandavyuha, Maitreya shows Sudhana a great tower holding a vision of infinite worlds, each with a Maitreya guiding beings, before the boy meets Samantabhadra.
In Japan his Fugen Enmei form, central to a longevity rite, is shown seated on a lotus held up by three elephants, or by one three-headed elephant.
The tenth of his great vows, dedicating all your merit to every being, became a common way to end Buddhist services in East Asia.
The novel Investiture of the Gods ends with Puxian Zhenren, Cihang Daoren and Wenshu Guangfa leaving the Daoist side and becoming the Buddhist figures Samantabhadra, Guanyin and Manjushri.
In the Lotus Sutra he teaches a protective dharani, and in the esoteric texts his seed syllable is Sam.
In the Avatamsaka Sutra he explains ten kinds of meditative absorption and ten supernormal powers, such as travelling freely to every realm in the universe.
In the Gandavyuha, Sudhana merges into Samantabhadra's body, which holds the entire universe, and Samantabhadra then recites his vows.
In the Avatamsaka Sutra, Samantabhadra teaches that Buddhahood is present in every particle of the physical universe and in the mind and body of every living being.
Asked two hundred questions about the bodhisattva path, he gives ten answers to each one, such as ten kinds of spiritual teachers and ten kinds of effort.
At Borobudur, the fourth gallery is entirely devoted to Samantabhadra's teaching, after Sudhana has met 53 teachers on his search.
In Nyingma Tibetan Buddhism the name Samantabhadra also belongs to a separate primordial Buddha, shown in union with a consort, Samantabhadri, who is not the bodhisattva of the same name.
The Kegon pilgrimage mandala preserved at Todai-ji in Nara pictures fifty-five saints, in which Fugen has a central role.

quiz.q: What animal does Samantabhadra ride in East Asian art?
options: A white elephant with six tusks
quiz.why: He is usually shown on a six-tusked white elephant.

quiz.q: Who does Sudhana meet at the end of his long journey in the Gandavyuha?
quiz.why: Sudhana meets Samantabhadra and, in the text, merges with him.

quiz.q: Which mountain in China is linked to Samantabhadra?
quiz.why: Mount Emei is his traditional seat and is 3,099 metres high.

quiz.q: How many great vows does Samantabhadra make in the Avatamsaka Sutra?
quiz.why: The sutra's closing chapter lists ten vows.
